title: The tannaim
hookLine: the sages of the Mishnah, from Hillel's time to Rabbi Judah the Prince

lines: RABBI MEIR SAYS. RABBI JUDAH SAYS.
ONE WORD FOR EACH OF THEM.
cards: Open the Mishnah almost anywhere and you hear a room full of people. Rabbi Meir says this. Rabbi Judah says that.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, and the sages say something else. The house of Shammai, the house of Hillel. Rabban Gamaliel, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Eliezer.
It reads less like a rulebook than the minutes of a very long meeting, with everyone's name attached to what they said. The Talmud has a single word for each of these teachers, and it's today's word.

teach.h: TANNA: ONE WHO REPEATS, AND TEACHES.
teach.b: Tanna. In the plural, tannaim. It's an Aramaic word, and Jastrow's dictionary of Talmudic Aramaic ties it to repeating, and so to teaching, because this teaching was learned by saying it over and over.

teach.h: HILLEL TO RABBI JUDAH THE PRINCE.
teach.b: The tannaim are the sages of the Mishnah, from Hillel and Shammai down to Rabbi Judah the Prince, who gathered their words. Hillel, patient. Shammai, strict.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who rebuilt after the Temple fell. Rabbi Akiva. And Rabbi Meir, a name the Talmud reads as one who gives light.

teach.h: MEIR: HE LIT UP THE SAGES' EYES.
teach.b: In tractate Eruvin it says that wasn't even his given name: he was called Meir because he lit up the eyes of the sages in the law. Now a surprise.
In tractate Sanhedrin, the Talmud says a teaching in the Mishnah with no name on it follows Rabbi Meir, and adds: all of them follow Rabbi Akiva, his teacher.

teach.h: UNSIGNED LINES STILL HAVE A TEACHER.
teach.b: Even the unsigned lines have a teacher behind them, and a teacher behind him.
A second surprise: the same word, tanna, also names a reciter in the house of study who had memorized great stores of teachings and could repeat them on request.
And the Talmud, in tractate Sotah, teases them, in paraphrase: the tanna recites and doesn't know what he's saying. Repeating isn't understanding. The tannaim gave the teaching its words.
Someone still had to explain them.

how: When Jews study the Mishnah they quote it by its teachers, saying 'Rabbi Meir says' or 'the sages say', and it is a custom to repeat a teaching in the name of the one who said it.

games.q: you're a student in an ancient house of study. you can recite a whole tractate word for word, but you can't explain a line of it. what would the Talmud call you?
o: a tanna who doesn't know what he's saying.
games.why: the Talmud in Sotah teases it: the tanna recites and doesn't know what he says. memory alone wasn't understanding.

practice: Breathe in on Rabbi and out on Meir, the one who gave light, and let the name settle the way a tanna settled a teaching, by repeating it until it's yours.
Then bring to mind someone who lit up a subject for you: a teacher, a parent, a coworker who explained what nobody else could. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Tanna. A teacher of the Mishnah, one of the sages from Hillel's time to Rabbi Judah the Prince, tied in the dictionary to repeating. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: a teacher of the Mishnah; plural tannaim, תַּנָּאִים.

carryVoice: Your line: the teachers of the mishnah. Their names stay attached to their words. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Marcus Jastrow, A Dictionary of the Targumim, the Talmud Babli and Yerushalmi, and the Midrashic Literature (1903), s.v. tana, tanna
